paras: The attempted lynching of Ely Thomas and Tim Zachary occurred on August 9, 1920, when a mob from Calhoun, Oklahoma, marched on the Le Flore County jail at Poteau to hang the two Black prisoners. Sheriff Fred Carter and his deputies drove both men out of town before the mob reached them, and they were lodged in the state penitentiary at McAlester. Thomas was convicted of murder less than a month later and sentenced to death.

Thomas was accused of shooting Selma Mayfield, a 21-year-old white farmer, as Mayfield rode past a Black picnic at Calhoun, a small mining town ten miles west of Poteau, on Saturday, August 7. According to the account given to officers, Thomas stepped into the road, asked Mayfield where he was going, and opened fire after Mayfield joked that he was "going to hell." The same account said that other Black picnickers disarmed Thomas and called the sheriff.

Zachary was charged with assaulting, or attempting to attack, the 16-year-old daughter of a farmer near Calhoun. The Mena Weekly Star said he was caught after he had "overpowered the girl early Monday morning," the day the mob formed.

Citizens of Calhoun held a mass meeting and voted to go to Poteau and "string up" the two men. The mob reached Poteau at about 9 o'clock that Monday morning and, instead of going straight to the jail, paraded the streets and urged residents to join it. During the parade Sheriff Carter, Chief Deputy D. G. Lane and deputies sworn in on the spot reached the jail by back alleys and put both prisoners into automobiles. The officers drove 15 miles to the Rock Island railroad, and that night both men were in the penitentiary at McAlester.
When the mob learned that the prisoners had a half-hour lead, it made no attempt to follow and "quietly dispersed." No one was hurt, and no arrests of mob members were reported.

Thomas was tried in the Le Flore County district court at Poteau, and on September 4 a jury found him guilty of murdering Mayfield and fixed the penalty at death by electrocution. The execution was set for November 23 at McAlester, and on September 18 the transcript of the case was placed before Governor Robertson and sent to the criminal court of appeals for review. No report of the outcome of Zachary's case was found in the coverage.

White newspapers in Oklahoma and Arkansas carried the story from August 10 to 12, mostly as a story of officers who outwitted a mob. The Mena Weekly Star headlined "Negroes in Close Call at Poteau" and credited the "instant and decisive action" of the authorities with preventing a "double lynching," calling the prisoners "two frightened men." The Guthrie Daily Leader likewise headlined "Sheriff Saves Two Negroes From Mob," but its subheads stated the charges as settled facts: "Attacked White Girl; Shot a Farmer." The Daily Ardmoreite put the alleged words of the shooting into its headline, "'I'll Send You to Hell' Negro Told Poteau Farmer as He Opened Fire," and in September called Thomas a "Murderer" in asking whether he would be pardoned.

The September conviction wire ran in Memphis and Pine Bluff, where the headline "Mob Forms When Negro is Convicted" described a mob that the text placed in August. The Black press appears only in a short Omaha Monitor item of September 9 that reported the death sentence for the murder of "a white farmer" and noted that Thomas had been removed when a mob "threatened violence." The Monitor printed the wire without comment, and no Black-press report of the August mob itself was found.

The Ardmore dispatch of August 9 differed from the other reports: it named only Thomas, said he had been taken in the night to Sallisaw before the mob arrived, and said Mayfield was expected to live. The other August reports, from two separate texts, put both men at McAlester that day and described Mayfield as killed or dying, and the later murder conviction is consistent with his death. Most reports dated the shooting August 7, while the Daily Ardmoreite's September story gave August 6.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Ely Thomas and Tim Zachary
bases: A mob gathered to hang two Black prisoners held in the Le Flore County jail at Poteau and was thwarted when officers removed them (A1, A3, A5).

A mob of Calhoun citizens set out to 'string up' Thomas and Zachary over a shooting and an alleged assault on a white girl, but officers moved both men before the mob reached them and no one was killed (A1, A3, A5).

At least two independent accounts, a short wire (A1, A4) and a separate Ardmore dispatch (A2), with a longer version in A3 and A5, agree that a mob came for the prisoners and that officers removed them; the Black press confirms it (A8).

framing.detail: The Mena Star's 'Negroes in Close Call at Poteau' and 'Infuriated Mob ... Frustrated From Double Lynching' praised the 'instant and decisive action' of the authorities and called the prisoners 'frightened men', while presenting the shooting from 'reports' and 'the report to officers'.
The Guthrie Daily Leader's headline 'Sheriff Saves Two Negroes From Mob' credited the sheriff, but its decks stated the charges as fact: 'Attacked White Girl; Shot a Farmer'.
The Daily Ardmoreite headlined the alleged words of the shooting as fact ('"I'll Send You to Hell" Negro Told Poteau Farmer'), and later labeled Thomas a 'Murderer'.
The September conviction wire ran in Memphis and Pine Bluff; the Pine Bluff headline 'Mob Forms When Negro is Convicted' described a mob not reported in the text.
The Omaha Monitor printed the conviction wire without comment, calling Mayfield 'a white farmer'.
